Adult individuals of the European sea squirt Ascidiella aspersa typically attain a maximum body length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the species' solitary growth form within the family Ascidiidae. The body, which is soft and saccular, is anchored to hard substrates in coastal waters, where it filters planktonic particles through its branchial basket. Sexual maturation begins well before this final size is reached; field surveys indicate that puberty, marked by the onset of gonad development, occurs when the individual reaches a body length of approximately 2.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 2.3 centimeters]. This relatively small size at the transition to reproductive competence suggests that Ascidiella aspersa allocates a substantial portion of its early growth to somatic tissue before diverting resources toward gamete production. In populations from the English Channel, the size at puberty shows limited variation, likely driven by consistent food availability in these tidally mixed waters. Newly hatched tadpole larvae, released after a brief embryonic period, are extremely small at birth, with a wet weight measured at just 0.000016 grams [Wwb = 0.000016 grams], a value consistent with the minute yolk reserves typical of ascidian larvae.

A series of controlled laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of a stable 20 °C [T = a stable 20 °C] provided detailed insights into the early life history of Ascidiella aspersa. Under these conditions, embryogenesis proceeds rapidly, and the free-swimming larva emerges from the fertilized egg capsule after only a single day (1 day) [ab = 1 day] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This remarkably short age at birth is characteristic of species with lecithotrophic, non-feeding larval stages that must quickly find a suitable settlement site. Once the larva attaches and undergoes metamorphosis, the resulting juvenile begins filter-feeding immediately. Under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum lifespan of this species under laboratory settings has been documented; individuals in captivity survive for up to 549 days [am = up to 549 days], a duration that corresponds to roughly 18 months and is typical for temperate ascidians with a relatively rapid pace of life. In the field, predation and physical disturbance likely reduce this survival period considerably.

When maintained in the laboratory at a constant temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C] with ad libitum food, reproductively active adults of Ascidiella aspersa display a substantial reproductive output. Under these warm-water conditions, individuals produce approximately 3,836 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3,836 eggs per day]. This high fecundity is consistent with the species' opportunistic life-history strategy, in which large numbers of small offspring are released to compensate for high larval mortality during the planktonic phase. The estimate derives from measured spawning events in aquarium-based studies, where gravid individuals released gametes synchronously. This daily rate, sustained over the reproductive season, can lead to a cumulative lifetime output numbering in the hundreds of thousands of eggs per individual. Although no separate data on clutch size and spawning frequency exist for this population, the combined daily rate provides a robust measure of reproductive potential.

The maximum wet weight achieved by fully grown adults of Ascidiella aspersa is approximately 31 grams [Wwi = approximately 31 grams], a mass that corresponds to the species' modest body dimensions. This ultimate wet weight, attained when the individual reaches the end of its exponential growth phase, is influenced by the structural composition of the tunic, which is largely composed of water and tunicin fibers. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Ascidiella scabra indicate that A. aspersa is the heavier of the two, likely as a result of its taller, more columnar body form. The relationship between body length and wet weight in this species is approximately cubic, consistent with isometric scaling of a roughly cylindrical organism. In benthic surveys, the largest individuals are typically found in sheltered harbors with low hydrodynamic stress, where they can grow to their full asymptotic mass without the risk of dislodgement. This mass also serves as the basis for estimating the species' reproductive output per unit body size.

Field studies tracking the reproductive cycle of Ascidiella aspersa have revealed that the onset of reproductive activity is linked to seasonal temperature cues. At the population level, the first spawning event of the year typically occurs when seawater temperatures rise above a threshold, and the age at this first reproduction has been estimated at approximately 5 months after settlement [tR = approximately 5 months after settlement]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive maturity allows multiple generations to be produced within a single warm season, a trait that facilitates rapid colonization of new substrates. The species is also known to exhibit a second, smaller spawning peak in late autumn if water temperatures remain elevated. The body length at puberty of 2.3 centimeters [Lp = 2.3 centimeters] that marks the onset of gonad development is consistent with the size at which the branchial basket reaches a filtering capacity sufficient to support both somatic maintenance and gametogenesis. This life-history pattern aligns with that of other opportunistic, short-lived ascidians common in epifaunal communities.
